newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Budget, monetary policy could hit sterling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Budget, monetary policy could hit sterling.

text.p: The prospect of a disappointing British budget and lower November inflation figures could be lying in wait to ambush runaway sterling, analysts said on Friday.
Sterling's rally accelerated this week after higher-than- expected inflation data for October fuelled speculation about another interest rate rise.

Economist Adam Cole of HSBC James Capel said he expected November retail prices data to be lower, however, which could help Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke avoid the rate rise the market seems to be banking on.
"If he didn't raise rates at all, he'd see sterling fall very rapidly," Cole said. "That would look much like the traditional sterling crisis, which is not what he wants in an election year."
The Conservative government of Prime Minister John Major must fight a general election before the end of May.

Given the poor state of Britain's public finances, a budget consisting of tax cuts without credible reductions in public spending would be viewed as negative for sterling, analysts said. Sterling powered ahead to a four-year high of $1.6697 against the dollar and a 30-month high of 2.5180 against the mark on Friday. Sterling's trade-weighted index rose to a 34-month high of 92.0.

The pound's latest sharp rise began on Wednesday after minutes of the September monetary meeting between Bank of England governor Eddie George and Clarke showed that George had urged the government to raise rates to over six percent.
Rates were last raised by a quarter of a percentage point to 6.0 percent on October 30.
October underlying retail prices data, which excludes home loan interest payments, showed a higher than expected 3.3 percent year-on-year rise in inflation.
Clarke said after the figures were released that the government's inflation target remained 2.5 percent, stoking speculation over an imminent rate rise.

Despite Cole's lower expectations for retail inflation, some other economists forecast underlying inflation would remain stagnant or rise to 3.4 percent in November. October's inflation figure was the highest rate for over three years.
Further clues about the strength of the economy are expected next week when Britain is scheduled to release data on money supply, gross domestic product and retail sales.
Cole said sterling would drift gradually downward to the low 2.40s against the mark after the next rate hike, which he expects in January.
"He will raise the rate -- probably by a quarter of a percentage point -- but not to the extent the market expects. We expect one increase, the market expects three," he said.
CIBC Wood Gundy's chief economist, David Coleman, agreed that sterling would continue to appreciate until there was another rate rise.

"Were there to be a decisive upward movement, it would help stem the speculation," he said. "You would probably see sterling spiking upward but I don't think that would continue once the market gets what it's looking for."

Coleman said sterling would remain firm at about 2.50 marks until the rate rise, which he forecast would follow the monthly monetary meeting between George and Clarke on December 11. "But a dreadful budget would help temper sterling's rise. The other thing would be a big retracement in the dollar, but that doesn't seem likely," he said. Clarke is due to present his budget to Parliament on November 26.
Coleman said Clarke seemed unconcerned about hurting exporters with his support for a strong pound because of the other benefits of sterling's appreciation.
"Sterling's going up does take some pressure off him to increase interest rates," he said. "And obviously, it does restrict import prices."
